claim: PM2.5 is defined as particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of less than 2.5 μm.
source: PM2.5 is defined as the aerodynamic diameter of less than 2.5 μm.
evidence: This is a standard definition in the field of environmental science and air quality research.

claim: PM2.5 has been proven to penetrate into the alveoli through inhalation and enter the systemic blood circulation.
source: PM2.5 has been proven to penetrate into the alveoli through inhalation, depositing on the alveolar wall and eventually enter the systemic blood circulation, leading to negative effects on primary organs, including the lung, cardiovascular, immune system, nervous system and genital system (Chu et al., 2019; Yue et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: PM2.5 has been classified as a known human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.
source: Moreover, the respirable particles have been classified as a known human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, with a growing number of studies uncovering the adverse effects in human and animals (Loomis et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to authoritative sources.

claim: The annual average PM2.5 level in China dropped from 67.4 μg/m3 in 2013 to 45.5 μg/m3 in 2017.
source: As a result, the annual average PM2.5 level in China dropped to 45.5 μg/m3 in 2017, compared to 67.4 μg/m3 in 2013 (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The 2021 average PM2.5 concentration in China was 6.5 times the World Health Organization's annual air quality guideline value.
source: However, according to the air quality monitoring system of the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) in cooperation with the Swiss technology company IQAir (https://www.iqair.com/), the 2021 average PM2.5 concentration in China was still 6.5 multiples of the World Health Organization's annual air quality guideline value.
evidence: Supported by reference to monitoring data from UNEP and IQAir.

claim: Exposure to PM2.5 during pregnancy leads to adverse pregnancy outcomes including placental dysfunction, ovarian dysfunction, impaired fetal development, lower birth weights, preterm births, reduced gestational age, congenital disability, and stillbirth.
source: Due to the toxic action of PM2.5, mounting evidence attests that exposure to PM2.5 during pregnancy leads to a variety of adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as placental dysfunction, ovarian dysfunction, impaired fetal development, lower birth weights, preterm births, reduced gestational age, congenital disability, and stillbirth (Zhou et al., 2020; Bekkar et al., 2020; Leung et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: PM2.5 exposure during gestation can adversely affect offspring health, including cardiovascular disease, respiratory damage, and neurodevelopmental impairment.
source: Exposure to PM2.5 during gestation can also have adversely effects on the health of the offspring, such as cardiovascular disease, respiratory damage, and neurodevelopmental impairment, as it has been reported that the etiology of many adult diseases may originate in the fetal period (Hart et al., 2021; Lavigne et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to research studies.

claim: PM2.5 can enter the circulating bloodstream through the alveolar wall and be deposited in the placenta.
source: In in vivo human placenta perfusion studies, the PM2.5 could enter the circulating bloodstream through the alveolar wall and deposited in the placenta, thus negatively affecting or even destroying placental function and creating a potential risk to the fetus (Martens et al., 2017; Michikawa et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to human placenta perfusion studies.

claim: Urban PM2.5 affects placental function, including placental thrombosis, chorioamnionitis, and inadequate trophoblast formation and invasion.
source: Previous studies have found that urban PM2.5 affects the function of the placenta, such as placental thrombosis, chorioamnionitis, and inadequate trophoblast formation and invasion, which adversely impacts fetal growth by interfering with mother-fetus interactions (Martens et al., 2017; Ghosh et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PM2.5 exposure during pregnancy induces abnormal alterations in placental genome DNA methylation profile.
source: PM2.5 exposure during pregnancy also induces abnormal alterations in the placental genome DNA methylation profile, which is primarily concentrated in genes associated with reproductive development, immune regulation and material metabolism (Nawrot et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study on DNA methylation.

claim: PM2.5 causes placental trophoblast cytotoxicity, impaired hormone regulation, inflammation and oxidative stress.
source: Moreover, Nääv Å et al. demonstrated that PM2.5 caused placental trophoblast cytotoxicity, impaired hormone regulation, inflammation and oxidative stress (Nääv et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: CYP1A1 plays an essential role in the metabolism of endogenous substrates such as hormones, melatonin, and inflammatory mediators.
source: As a cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme, CYP1A1 plays an essensial role in the metabolism of endogenous substrates (such as hormones 17β estradiol [Kisselev et al., 2005], melatonin [Goh et al., 2021], inflammatory mediators arachidonic acid [Sroczyńska et al., 2022] and eicosapentaenoic acid [Schwarz et al., 2004]) and exogenous substrates (such as PAHs [Chen et al., 2022b], doxin [Molcan et al., 2017], and halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons [Kasai et al., 2008]).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on CYP1A1 metabolism.

claim: CYP1A1 converts benzo[a]pyrene into the carcinogenic 7,8-dihydroxy-9,10-epoxybenzo[a]pyrene through multiple oxidation steps.
source: For example, CYP1A1 converts benzo[a]pyrene into the carcinogenic 7,8-dihydroxy-9,10-epoxybenzo[a]pyrene by multiple oxidation steps which causes severe oxidative damage to cells by generating excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Zajda et al., 2019; Gastelum et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on CYP1A1-mediated metabolism.

claim: PM2.5 contributes to the increase of CYP1A1 in human neutrophils, bronchial epithelial cells, and alveolar macrophages.
source: It has been proven that PM2.5 contributes to the increase of CYP1A1 in human neutrophils, bronchial epithelial cells, and alveolar macrophage due to the adsorption of adsorbs aromatic hydrocarbons on their surface, which in-turn inducing oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and apoptosis (Chen et al., 2019; Van Winkle et al., 2015; Abbas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on PM2.5 effects on CYP1A1.

claim: PM2.5 induced malformations in zebrafish embryonic heart development by activating CYP1A1.
source: Yue C et al. also found that PM2.5 induced malformations in zebrafish embryonic heart development by activating CYP1A1 (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a zebrafish study.

claim: The PM2.5 particles collected in this study were primarily flocculent in shape, with only a few flakes and rods.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, we explicitly observed that the PM2.5 particles had randomly aggregated and scattered in the field of view, with most of them being less than 2.5 μm in length. The particles were primarily flocculent in shape, with only a few flakes and rods.
evidence: Directly observed in SEM images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The elements O, N, and C were predominantly present in the collected PM2.5, with other elements such as Cl, Si, S, Al, and Ni also detected.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the elements O, N, and C were predominantly present, while other elements such as Cl, Si, and the heavy metals S, Al, and Ni were also detected.
evidence: Detected by EDS analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The proportion of elements in PM2.5 displayed the following trend: O>N > C>Cl > Si>S > Na>K > Al>Ca > Ni.
source: The proportion of the elements displayed the following trend: O>N > C>Cl > Si>S > Na>K > Al>Ca > Ni.
evidence: Based on EDS analysis of PM2.5 composition.

claim: PM2.5 treatment resulted in a significant reduction in fetal numbers, embryo resorption, and increased stillbirths in mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2B and C, PM2.5 treatment resulted in a significant reduction in fetal numbers, embryo resorption, and the increase of stillbirths (n=8).
evidence: Observed in mouse experiments shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The weight of the placenta of pregnant mice was decreased after PM2.5 treatment.
source: The weight of the placenta of the pregnant mice was also decreased.
evidence: Measured in mouse experiments.

claim: PM2.5 exposure resulted in loosely distributed and disorganized cells in the labyrinth layer of mouse placenta, with more vacuoles and larger intercellular gaps.
source: Notably, compared with the control group, the cells of the labyrinth layer in the PM2.5-exposed group were loosely distributed, and disorganized, with more vacuoles and larger intercellular gaps.
evidence: Observed in HE staining of placental tissue.

claim: PM2.5 exposure resulted in reduced distribution of placental capillaries and significantly lower number of red blood cells in mouse placenta.
source: The distribution of the placental capillaries was reduced and the number of red blood cells was significantly lower.
evidence: Observed in HE staining of placental tissue.

claim: PM2.5 exposure resulted in increased levels of apoptosis in mouse placental labyrinth cells, primarily in trophoblasts.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, PM2.5 exposure resulted in increased levels of apoptosis in the mouse placental labyrinth cells compared with the normal group, with apoptosis being primarily observed in the trophoblasts of the mouse placental labyrinth.
evidence: Detected by TUNEL staining shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PM2.5 decreased the expression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 and increased the expression of the pro-apoptotic proteins BAX and Cleaved-caspase 3 in mouse placenta.
source: The expression of apoptosis-related proteins including cleaved-caspase 3, BCL-2 and BAX were measured using western blotting (n=3), which also confirmed the increased levels of apoptosis in the placenta of PM2.5-exposed mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Measured by western blotting shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PM2.5 particles significantly changed the morphology of HTR8/SVneo cells, with cells becoming swollen and deformed with a large number of vacuoles in the cytoplasm.
source: Transmission electron microscopy clearly indicated that PM2.5 particles significantly changed the morphology of the cells (Figure 3A). Compared with the control group, the PM2.5-exposed cells were swollen and deformed, with a large number of vacuoles in the cytoplasm, and with mitochondria exhibiting visibly damaged intracellular ultrastructure.
evidence: Observed by transmission electron microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PM2.5 exposure caused mitochondria in HTR8/SVneo cells to become round or oval, with reduced volume, thickened matrix, inconspicuous cristae, and dense precipitated material.
source: The mitochondria in the cells of the PM2.5-exposed group were round or oval, with some becoming solid. The mitochondrial volume was reduced, the matrix was thickened, the cristaes were inconspicuous, and the interior of the mitochondria were precipitated with dense, indefinite material.
evidence: Observed by transmission electron microscopy.

claim: PM2.5 could be taken up by HTR8/SVneo cells as evidenced by increased SSC-A values in flow cytometry.
source: Flow cytometry was used to assess whether cells had taken up PM2.5 based on the changes of the SSC-A (Side Scatter Area) values (Zhao and Ibuki, 2015). As shown in Figure 3B, the FSC-A remained largely the same as the control group after PM2.5 treatment, but the SSC-A increased significantly in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: Measured by flow cytometry shown in Figure 3B, with citation to methodology.

claim: PM2.5 significantly inhibited HTR8/SVneo cell proliferation in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: CCK-8 assays showed that PM2.5 significantly inhibited cell proliferation with a concentration-dependent way (Figure 3C).
evidence: Measured by CCK-8 assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When PM2.5 concentration reached 100 μg/mL, HTR8/SVneo cell proliferation decreased by nearly 50%.
source: When the PM2.5 concentration reached 100 μg/mL, cell proliferation decreased by nearly 50%.
evidence: Measured by EDU staining assays.

claim: PM2.5 significantly increased HTR8/SVneo cell apoptosis.
source: Annexin V-FITC/PI staining and flow cytometry analysis were used to detect cell apoptosis and it was found that PM2.5 significantly increased cell apoptosis (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Measured by Annexin V-FITC/PI staining and flow cytometry shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: PM2.5-exposed HTR8/SVneo cells migrated more slowly compared to control group.
source: The wound healing assay was carried out to assess the migration of HTR8/SVneo cells. The results indicated that the cells in the PM2.5-exposed group migrated more slowly compared to the corresponding migration rate in the control group (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: Measured by wound healing assay shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: The invasive activity of PM2.5-exposed HTR8/SVneo cells was significantly reduced.
source: In support of this, the Transwell invasion assays showed that the invasive activity of PM2.5-exposed HTR8/SVneo cells was significantly reduced, with very few cells visible across the bottom membrane at PM2.5 concentrations up to 200 μg/mL (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: Measured by Transwell invasion assays shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: PM2.5 had a detrimental effect on angiogenesis in HTR8/SVneo cells, with cells largely unable to form lumen structures at 200 μg/mL.
source: Finally, we detected the angiogenic ability of HTR8/SVneo cells, a process that mimics the formation of blood vessels after trophoblast invades the endometrium (Belyakova et al., 2019). As expected, PM2.5 had a detrimental effect on angiogenesis in trophoblast cells, and we found that at PM2.5 concentrations of 200 μg/mL, cells were largely unable to form lumen structures (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: Measured by tube formation assay shown in Figure 3L and M, with citation to context.

claim: RNA-Seq analysis identified 32 differentially expressed coding genes between control and PM2.5 treatment groups, comprising 24 up-regulated genes and 8 down-regulated genes.
source: By applying the cut-off criteria of Q value﹤0.05 and |log2[Fold Change]|≥1, we identified 32 coding genes that exhibited differential expression between the control and PM2.5 treatment groups, comprising 24 up-regulated genes and 8 down-regulated genes.
evidence: Based on RNA-Seq analysis with specified statistical criteria.

claim: GSEA revealed significant upregulation of cytochrome P450 pathway, chemical carcinogenesis pathway, ovarian steroidogenesis pathway and steroid biosynthesis pathway in PM2.5-exposed group.
source: Our findings were further supported by GSEA, which revealed significant upregulation of four enriched pathways - cytochrome P450 pathway, chemical carcinogenesis pathway, ovarian steroidogenesis pathway and Steroid biosynthesis pathway - in the PM2.5-exposed group (Figure 4E).
evidence: Based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cytochrome P450 is the most significantly enriched pathway affected by PM2.5 in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: The results from both analyses suggest that cytochrome P450 is the most significantly enriched pathway.
evidence: Based on KEGG enrichment analysis and GSEA results.

claim: PM2.5 exposure resulted in a significant decrease in GSH and SOD levels and a considerable increase in MDA levels in mouse placental tissues.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, PM2.5 exposure resulted in a significant decrease in GSH and SOD level and a considerable increase in MDA levels in the mouse placental tissues (n=8).
evidence: Measured in mouse placental tissues shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PM2.5 exposure resulted in reduced expression of antioxidant proteins HO-1, NQO-1, GCLC, and SOD-1 in mouse placenta.
source: We further detected the expression of the antioxidant proteins heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NADPH quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO-1), glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCLC), and superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD-1) in mice placenta by western blotting. The results showed that PM2.5 exposure resulted in reduced expression of these antioxidant proteins in the placenta (n=3) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Measured by western blotting shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PM2.5 exposure reduced the expression of antioxidant proteins HO-1, NQO-1, GCLC, and SOD-1 in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: Additionally, the expression of the antioxidant proteins HO-1, NQO-1, GCLC, and SOD-1 was reduced after PM2.5 exposure in the placental trophoblast cell line HTR8/SVneo cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Measured by western blotting shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PM2.5 exposure caused a significant increase in ROS levels in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: The ROS levels were measured by cellular immunofluorescence staining and flow cytometry, and the results showed that there was a significant increase in the PM2.5-exposed cells (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Measured by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: PM2.5 exposure caused a considerable increase in mitochondrial ROS levels in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: Therefore, we detected the mitochondrial ROS levels using the Mito-SOX probe. The results revealed a considerable increase in the level of ROS in the mitochondria with increasing PM2.5 concentration (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Measured using Mito-SOX probe shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: PM2.5 exposure caused a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: The JC-1 probe was used to detect changes in the levels of the mitochondrial membrane potential. As shown in the Figure 5I and J, the mitochondrial membrane potential in the control group of HTR8/SVneo cells was high, and after the addition of PM2.5, the red fluorescence of JC-1 diminished and gradually showed green fluorescence, representing a decrease in the mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: Measured using JC-1 probe shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: PM2.5 induced the translocation of cytochrome C from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: Consistently, we extracted and separated the mitochondrial proteins and cytoplasmic proteins to examine the expression of mitochondrial apoptosis-related proteins via western blotting. The results indicated that PM2.5 induced the translocation of cytochrome C from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm, and the expression of BCL-2 was decreased, whilst BAX and cleaved-caspase 3 expression were elevated (Figure 5K).
evidence: Measured by western blotting of mitochondrial and cytoplasmic fractions shown in Figure 5K.

claim: NAC reversed the PM2.5-induced decrease in GSH and SOD levels and increase in MDA production in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: The addition of NAC simultaneously increased intracellular GSH and SOD levels, and diminished MDA production (Figure 6A).
evidence: Measured in NAC rescue experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NAC reduced the elevated ROS levels caused by PM2.5 in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: Cellular immunofluorescence and flow cytometry revealed that NAC reduced the elevated ROS levels caused by PM2.5 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Measured by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: NAC reversed PM2.5-induced cell dysfunction in proliferation, apoptosis, invasion and angiogenesis in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: NAC also resulted in the reverse of cell dysfunction on the proliferation, apoptosis, invasion and angiogenesis when compared with the PM2.5 exposed group (from Figure 6D to M)
evidence: Measured by multiple assays shown in Figures 6D to M.

claim: NAC reversed the PM2.5-induced increase in pro-apoptotic proteins BAX and cleaved-caspase 3 and prevented the transfer of cytochrome C from mitochondria to cytoplasm.
source: The results of western blotting indicated that the addition of NAC reversed the PM2.5-induced increase in the expression of the pro-apoptotic proteins BAX and cleaved-caspase 3 and prevented the transfer of cytochrome C from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm, whilst increasing the expression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 (Figure 6N).
evidence: Measured by western blotting shown in Figure 6N.

claim: CYP1A1 expression was most significantly elevated among CYP1A1, CYP1B1 and ALDH1A3 after PM2.5 exposure in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: KEGG enrichment analysis showed that PM2.5 had the most significant effect on the metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450, primarily affecting CYP1A1, CYP1B1 and ALDH1A3 (Figure 4D). The proteins encoded by these three genes were detected by western blotting, and the results showed that CYP1A1 expression was most significantly elevated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured by western blotting shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: CYP1A1 expression was significantly increased in mouse placental tissue after PM2.5 exposure.
source: To investigate the role of CYP1A1 in PM2.5-induced defects, we first examined the expression of CYP1A1 in mice placental tissue by immunofluorescence staining and western blotting (Figure 7A and B). The results showed that, compared to the control group, the expression of CYP1A1 was significantly increased by PM2.5 exposure.
evidence: Measured by immunofluorescence and western blotting shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: CYP1A1 mRNA transcripts and protein levels were elevated in PM2.5-exposed HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: Similarly, in PM2.5-exposed HTR8/Svneo cells, the levels of CYP1A1 mRNA transcripts and protein were both elevated as revealed by qRT-PCR (Figure 7C), immunofluorescence staining (Figure 7D) and western blotting (Figure 7E)
evidence: Measured by qRT-PCR, immunofluorescence, and western blotting shown in Figure 7C, D, and E.

claim: Knockdown of CYP1A1 reduced the elevated levels of ROS caused by PM2.5 in HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: The results showed that the elevated levels of ROS caused by PM2.5 were reduced following CYP1A1 knockdown (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: Measured after CYP1A1 knockdown shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: Knockdown of CYP1A1 reduced the elevated mitochondrial ROS levels caused by PM2.5 in HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: The elevated mitochondrial ROS levels caused by PM2.5 were also reduced after CYP1A1 knockdown as shown by the Mito-SOX staining (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: Measured by Mito-SOX staining shown in Figure 7I and J.

claim: Knockdown of CYP1A1 reversed the decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential caused by PM2.5 in HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: Meanwhile, JC-1 staining also revealed that the knockdown of CYP1A1 reversed the decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential caused by PM2.5 (Figure 7K and L).
evidence: Measured by JC-1 staining shown in Figure 7K and L.

claim: Knockdown of CYP1A1 reversed PM2.5-induced changes in mitochondrial apoptosis-related proteins in HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: Western blotting results showed that PM2.5 led to a decrease in BCL-2 expression, an increase in BAX expression, the translocation of cytochrome C from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm and the activation of downstream cleaved-caspase3 expression. When CYP1A1 was knocked down, these changes were significantly reversed (Figure 7M).
evidence: Measured by western blotting shown in Figure 7M.

claim: Knockdown of CYP1A1 reversed PM2.5-induced impairment of HTR8/Svneo biological functions including proliferation, invasion, migration, and angiogenesis.
source: Furthermore, we tested whether the knockdown of CYP1A1 reduced the effect of PM2.5 on the biological functions of HTR8/Svneo cells. EDU, Annexin V-FITC/PI staining, wound-healing, Transwell and tube formation assays results suggested that CYP1A1 knockdown can reverse PM2.5-induced impairment of HTR8/Svneo biological functions, such as proliferation, invasion, migration, angiogenesis, and apoptosis (Figure 8).
evidence: Measured by multiple functional assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: The half-lives of CYP1A1 mRNA in PM2.5-exposed and non-exposed groups were 5.62 hr and 7.08 hr respectively, with no significant difference.
source: RNA-Seq showed that PM2.5 could regulate CYP1A1 expression at the transcriptional level, so we examined the stability of CYP1A1 mRNA by qRT-PCR after treatment with actinomycin D to determine whether the increase in CYP1A1 expression was related to its post-transcriptional regulation by PM2.5. The results showed that the half-lives of CYP1A1 mRNA in the PM2.5-exposed and non-exposed groups were 5.62 hr and 7.08 hr, respectively, and the difference was not significant (Figure 9A).
evidence: Measured by mRNA degradation assay shown in Figure 9A.

claim: PM2.5 enhanced the transcriptional activity of CYP1A1 promoter in HTR8/SVneo cells.
source: We then assessed the transcriptional activity of the CYP1A1 promoter using a dual luciferase reporter assay and found enhanced transcriptional activity of CYP1A1 in the PM2.5 exposed cells compared with the control cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: Measured by dual luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 9B.

claim: KLF9 emerged as the only potential transcription factor that could bind to the CYP1A1 promoter region when predicted transcription factors were mapped to RNA-Seq differentially expressed genes.
source: Using the JASPAR database (https://jaspar.genereg.net/), HOCOMOCO MoLoTool (https://molotool.autosome.org/), and the hTFtarget database (http://bioinfo.life.hust.edu.cn/hTFtarget#!/), we predicted dozens of TFs that could bind to the CYP1A1 promoter region (TSS, –532/+88). Interestingly, these TFs were further confined when mapped to the DEGs in the RNA-Seq data, and KLF9 emerged as the only potential TF.
evidence: Based on bioinformatics analysis using multiple databases and RNA-Seq data.

claim: Over-expression of KLF9 increased the transcriptional activity of CYP1A1.
source: Notably, the dual-luciferase assay revealed that over-expression of KLF9 increased the transcriptional activity of CYP1A1 (Figure 9F).
evidence: Measured by dual-luciferase assay shown in Figure 9F.

claim: A response element of the CYP1A1 promoter located in the –64 bp to –49 bp region (GAAGGAGGCGTGGCC) is required for transcription of CYP1A1 mediated by KLF9.
source: We found that mutation of either site#1 (-456 bp to –440 bp) or mutation site #2 (-162 bp to –146 bp) did not affect the promotive effect of KLF9 on the transcription of CYP1A1, but this was not the case for site #3 (-64 bp to –49 bp). Consistently, further simultaneous mutation of the three sites resulted in an abrogation of the promotive effect of KLF9 (Figure 9F). These results suggested that a response element of the CYP1A1 promoter located in the –64 bp to –49 bp region, GAAGGAGGCGTGGCC, was required for the transcription of of CYP1A1 meditated by KLF9.
evidence: Measured by dual-luciferase assay with mutant constructs shown in Figure 9F.

claim: KLF9 can bind directly to the CYP1A1 promoter.
source: Subsequently, we investigated the binding of KLF9 to the CYP1A1 promoter using ChIP analysis. The chromatin was precipitated with antibodies specific for KLF9 or IgG, and PCR analysis with the primers (spanning the –96/+16 bp region of the CYP1A1 promoter) showed that KLF9 was able to bind directly to the CYP1A1 promoter (Figure 9G and H).
evidence: Measured by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 9G and H.

claim: There is a positive correlation between KLF9 and CYP1A1 expression in the trophoblast layer of human placental tissue.
source: Furthermore, we observed a positive correlation between KLF9 and CYP1A1 expression in the trophoblast layer of human placental tissue by immunohistochemical fluorescence co-staining in 30 randomly selected pregnant placental tissues in the clinic (Figure 9I and J).
evidence: Measured by immunohistochemical fluorescence co-staining in human placental tissues shown in Figure 9I and J.

claim: KLF9 expression in mouse placenta was markedly increased in response to PM2.5 stimulation, particularly in the labyrinth layer.
source: To investigate the possible role of KLF9 in PM2.5-induced trophoblast dysfunction, we first demonstrated that KLF9 expression in mouse placenta was markedly increased in response to PM2.5 stimulation, particularly in the labyrinth layer (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: Measured by immunofluorescence and western blotting shown in Figure 10A and B.

claim: The expression of KLF9 in HTR8/Svneo cells was increased by PM2.5 treatment.
source: Mirroring the findings in mice, the expression of KLF9 in HTR8/Svneo cells was increased by PM2.5 treatment (Figure 10C).
evidence: Measured by western blotting shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The increase in KLF9 expression after PM2.5 treatment was primarily observed in the nucleus of HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: Cellular immunofluorescence showed that the increase in KLF9 expression was primarily observed in the nucleus (Figure 10D).
evidence: Observed by cellular immunofluorescence shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Knockdown of KLF9 abrogated the increase in intracellular ROS levels induced by PM2.5 in HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: Next, we knocked down the expression of KLF9 by two siRNAs in HTR8/Svneo cells. Using DCFH-DA, we found that the knockdown of KLF9 abrogated the increase in intracellular ROS levels induced by PM2.5 (Figure 10E and F).
evidence: Measured after KLF9 knockdown shown in Figure 10E and F.

claim: KLF9 knockdown prevented mitochondrial ROS production induced by PM2.5 in HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: KLF9 knockdown also prevented mitochondrial ROS production (Figure 10G1)
evidence: Measured after KLF9 knockdown shown in Figure 10G.

claim: KLF9 knockdown resulted in an increase in mitochondrial potential in PM2.5-exposed HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: KLF9 knockdown also prevented mitochondrial ROS production (Figure 10G1), resulted in an increase in mitochondrial potential (Figure 10H and J)
evidence: Measured after KLF9 knockdown shown in Figure 10H and J.

claim: KLF9 knockdown blocked the translocation of cytochrome C from mitochondria to cytoplasm and reduced mitochondrial apoptosis in PM2.5-exposed HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: KLF9 knockdown also prevented mitochondrial ROS production (Figure 10G1), resulted in an increase in mitochondrial potential (Figure 10H and J), and blocked the translocation of cytochrome C from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm. As a result, mitochondrial apoptosis was also reduced by KLF9 knockdown as revealed by the upregulation of BCL-2 expression, downregulation of BAX and cleaved-caspase 3 expression (Figure 10K).
evidence: Measured by western blotting after KLF9 knockdown shown in Figure 10K.

claim: Knockdown of KLF9 abrogated the disruption of trophoblast function by PM2.5 in HTR8/Svneo cells.
source: Consistently, knockdown of KLF9 also abrogated the disruption of trophoblast function by PM2.5 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B–I).
evidence: Measured by multiple functional assays shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B–I.

claim: The suppression actions by KLF9 silencing on PM2.5-induced mitochondrial apoptosis were restored by CYP1A1 overexpression.
source: To delineate the link between KLF9 and CYP1A1 after PM2.5 exposure, KLF9 was then knocked down in PM2.5-exposed HTR8/Svneo cultured with lentivirus-mediated ectopic expression of CYP1A1. Notably, the suppression actions by KLF9 silencing on PM2.5-induced mitochondrial apoptosis were restored by CYP1A1 overexpression, suggesting the effect of KLF9 in regulating mitochondrial apoptosis was mediated by CYP1A1 (Figure 10L).
evidence: Measured by western blotting in rescue experiments shown in Figure 10L.

claim: PM2.5 causes oxidative stress damage and mitochondrial apoptosis with impairment of cell biological functions through the KLF9/CYP1A1 signaling pathway in HTR8/SVneo.
source: In conclusion, the results confirmed that PM2.5 caused oxidative stress damage, and mitochondrial apoptosis with impairment of cell biological functions through the KLF9/CYP1A1 signaling pathway in HTR8/SVneo.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive experimental results presented in the study.

claim: The KLF9/CYP1A1 axis plays a crucial role in the toxic progression of PM2.5 induced adverse pregnancy outcomes.
source: Together, this study demonstrated that the KLF9/CYP1A1 axis played a crucial role in the toxic progression of PM2.5 induced adverse pregnancy outcomes, suggesting adverse effects of environmental pollution on pregnant females and putative targeted therapeutic strategies.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive experimental results presented in the study.

claim: The PM2.5 exposure dosage for mice was calculated by combining PM2.5 exposure levels of pregnant women in Jinan with physiological indicators of mice, multiplied by a 100-fold uncertainty factor.
source: We combined the PM2.5 exposure level of pregnant women from the Jinan (Wang et al., 2022) (where we collected PM2.5 particles) with physiological indicators of mice (Vermillion et al., 2018), then multiplied by 100-fold uncertainty factor to obtain the corresponding PM2.5 exposure dosage during mice pregnancy.
evidence: Based on established toxicological methodology with citations to relevant studies.

claim: The 100-fold uncertainty factor is used to convert a no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) from an animal toxicity study to a safe value for human intake (ADI).
source: The 100-fold uncertainty factor ( =10 fold interspecies difference ×10 fold interindividual variation) is used to convert a no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) from an animal toxicity study to a safe value for human intake (ADI), which is the criteria for determining experimental dosages in toxicological studies involving animals.
evidence: This is an established principle in toxicology.

claim: The 100-fold uncertainty factor was originally proposed over 60 years ago by Lehman and Fitzhugh, 1954.
source: It was originally proposed, over 60 years ago, by Lehman and Fitzhugh, 1954, and still forms the basis of the uncertainty factors which are in use today.
evidence: Supported by citation to the original proposal.

claim: HTR8/SVneo cells are a more suitable model for studying trophoblast function than choriocarcinoma BeWo, JEG-3, and JAR cells.
source: HTR8/SVneo cells are perpetuated by the SV40 Tag and not only maintain many of the essential and key features of the parental cells, but are also devoid of any features of neoplastic transformation (Bilban et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2021). Therefore, HTR8/SVneo cells are a more suitable model for this study than choriocarcinoma BeWo, JEG-3, and JAR cells.
evidence: Based on established characteristics of the cell line with citations.

claim: Organic pollutants on the surface of PM2.5 can lead to the development of oxidative stress in cells.
source: Studies have shown that the toxicological effects of PM2.5 on cells could depend on the pollutant composition of PM2.5. In particular, organic pollutants can lead towards the development of oxidative stress in cells.
evidence: Based on general knowledge from previous studies.

claim: PM2.5 containing benzo[b]fluoranthene, chrysene, and fluoranthene impairs the antioxidant system of lung epithelial cells, leading to increased cellular ROS levels and reduced cellular activity.
source: For example, PM2.5 containing benzo[b]fluoranthene, chrysene, and fluoranthene impair the antioxidant system of lung epithelial cells, leading to increased cellular ROS levels and reduced cellular activity Deng et al., 2013
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Exposure to PM2.5 containing high concentrations of metals and polar organic compounds can lead to elevated levels of 8-OHdG in urine and elevated levels of oxidative stress.

source: For example, CYP1A1 induction enhanced gefitinib-induced oxidative stress and apoptosis in A549 cells and was implicated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Callaway et al., 2020).

source: Furthermore, aromatic hydrocarbons in PM2.5 could increase the expression level of CYP1A1, inducing oxidative stress and inflammation in several cells, such as human bronchial epithelial cells (Gu et al., 2021), neutrophils (Vogel et al., 2016), and epithelial cells (Toydemir et al., 2021), amongst others.

source: For example, AHR is an essential ligand-activated transcription factor of the cytochrome P450 pathway, controlling the expression of CYP1A1, CYP1B1, CYP1A2 and other genes in the cytochromes P450 family (Torti et al., 2021; Al-Dhfyan et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2021).

claim: AHR could be activated by many environmental pollutants, including PM2.5.

source: Importantly, our study has revealed that KLF9 exerted a positive regulatory effect on CYP1A1 in humans, which is in contrast to its previously reported transcriptional repression of CYP1A1 in rat liver.
evidence: Based on the experimental results in this study compared to previous rat studies.
